description: Fake airdrop claim scam: the transaction invokes an unverified program under the guise of claiming rewards or an airdrop, but includes a hidden instruction transferring SPL tokens or SOL out to an attacker wallet. Classic drainer pattern.

Token account authority takeover (SetAuthority): the transaction calls SPL Token SetAuthority to change the owner or close authority of the user's token account to an untrusted external address, permanently revoking user ownership.

Unbounded token approval delegate drain: the transaction executes SPL Token Approve or ApproveChecked with a massive or u64::MAX allowance to an unverified third-party account, enabling the delegate to drain the user's tokens asynchronously.
Account close rent sweep: the transaction calls SPL Token CloseAccount on the user's token account and routes the recovered rent lamports to an unrecognized destination rather than the wallet owner.
Native SOL sweep drainer: the transaction calls System Program Transfer to move almost the entire SOL balance to an unverified recipient with zero prior interaction history.

DEX impersonation scam: an unverified custom program mimics a popular DEX router like Jupiter or Raydium, but instead of executing liquidity pool swaps, diverts input tokens into an attacker's treasury.

Malicious CPI flash drain: an unverified custom contract executes cross-program invocations to legitimate protocols while passing unauthorized recipient accounts, siphoning flash-loaned or user collateral.
Full drainer combo: a transaction calling an unverified program alongside an SPL Token Approve for maximum allowance and a System Program transfer, maximizing total asset drainage in one signature.
Standard token swap: the transaction routes through Jupiter v6 or Raydium AMM to swap SOL for USDC or another token across audited liquidity pools. Routine, safe DEX activity.
Self transfer: a simple System Program Transfer sending SOL between the user's own addresses or funding an associated token account. Carries no counterparty risk.
Lending deposit: the transaction deposits SOL or USDC into Kamino Lending, Solend, or Marginfi with standard collateral minting. Audited protocol with well-defined withdrawal rights.
Liquid staking: depositing SOL into Marinade or Jito to receive mSOL or JitoSOL via verified on-chain stake pools.
Compute budget optimization: transaction prepends ComputeBudget instructions (SetComputeUnitLimit, SetComputeUnitPrice) to pay priority fees for faster confirmation. Standard benign practice.
Multi-hop swap with lending: swapping SOL for USDC on Jupiter and immediately supplying it as collateral on Kamino Lending. Common multi-protocol composition across audited contracts.
First-time interaction with newly deployed program: an instruction calls a program ID not yet registered in verified protocol lists. Requires caution even if no obvious drain pattern is present.
Large outbound SOL transfer: transferring a substantial amount of SOL (>50 SOL) to a known counterparty or exchange deposit address.
